summary: B is substantially closer to the frozen contract and far more scope-disciplined. A changes the required API type, adds expressly prohibited association machinery, and refactors retry behavior unrelated to the prescribed solution.
reasons: B implements the exact required signature: Upload(ctx context.Context, fileName string, content io.Reader, opts ...FilesOption). A instead exposes opts ...UploadFileOption, violating the public API contract and changing how existing FilesOption values apply.

B directly reuses internal/multipartbody.NewFile("file", fileName, content), producing the required replayable buffered body. A introduces NewFileWithFields and expands the internal helper for functionality the contract explicitly excludes.
A adds association options and arbitrary multipart fields despite the explicit instruction not to add association fields or change FilesOption behavior.

A changes RawClient request/retry and body-closing semantics globally, including Files.Add and Update, despite the contract requiring preservation of Add behavior and no unrelated retry refactor. B leaves that machinery untouched and solves replayability within Upload as requested.DETAILS can be found in the risks_a field below.DESCRIPTION can be found in the risks_b field below.
risks_a: Upload does not accept the required ...FilesOption type; ordinary FilesOption implementations are no longer necessarily usable with it.
The new UploadFileOption/FilesRequestOption hierarchy changes exported option APIs and return types, creating avoidable compatibility and maintenance risk.

The association fields, WithFileFormField, multipart helper expansion, changelog claims, README changes, and global seekable-body machinery are out of scope and contradict explicit contract constraints. The implementation also bypasses FilesService.Add instead of routing through it and lacks a source-reader error test.
risks_b: Upload duplicates Add's option handling, request construction, response decoding, and missing-data error instead of calling s.Add(ctx, body, contentType, opts...), violating the required single-path design and risking future semantic drift.

Tests do not cover propagation of a failing source reader. The retry test also starts with bytes.NewReader rather than a more clearly streamed source, although it does verify replay of the multipart body after a 429.
